modules.label: Fundamentals
modules.summary: Voice AI is three components stitched together under a brutal latency budget — everything else in the field is a variation on that.

lessons.title: The three building blocks of a voice agent
lessons.why: Every voice AI pitch, Deepgram's or Sierra's, is a variation on how these three pieces are arranged.
facts: ASR (automatic speech recognition): audio in, text out — turns what the caller said into words.
The reasoning layer: an LLM or dialogue manager that decides what to say back.
TTS (text-to-speech): text in, audio out — turns the response into a voice the caller hears.

lessons.title: ASR: what it actually does
lessons.why: Worth understanding as its own component, not just as 'step one' of the pipeline.
facts: Its whole job is turning audio into accurate text, fast enough to feed a live conversation.
Word error rate (WER) is the standard accuracy metric — the percentage of words transcribed wrong.
Accuracy depends heavily on accent, background noise, and domain-specific vocabulary — a model that scores well on clean, standard-accent audio can degrade a lot on a real phone line.

lessons.title: TTS: what it actually does
lessons.why: The other bookend of the pipeline — often under-discussed compared to ASR and the LLM.
facts: Its job is turning text into audio that sounds natural enough to hold a caller's attention and trust.
Modern TTS uses neural vocoders, producing far more natural prosody (rhythm, intonation) than older concatenative or parametric synthesis.
Like ASR, it runs under a real-time constraint — time-to-first-byte on the audio output matters as much as how natural it sounds.

lessons.title: Cascaded vs. speech-to-speech architectures
lessons.why: This is the single biggest architectural fork in the industry right now, and both Sierra and Deepgram sit on opposite defaults.
facts: Cascaded: ASR, LLM, and TTS are separate models/services stitched together — flexible, debuggable, easier to add business logic between steps.
Speech-to-speech (STS): a single model processes audio in and audio out directly, without a text intermediate — lower latency, more natural turn-taking, but a harder-to-inspect 'black box'.

Deepgram's Voice Agent API is a hybrid: it bundles STT + TTS + LLM orchestration behind one WebSocket connection so teams get a single integration without giving up the cascaded model's inspectability.

lessons.title: Cascaded architecture, in depth
lessons.why: Still the dominant architecture in production voice agents — worth knowing exactly why it's dominant, not just that it is.
facts: Each stage (ASR, LLM, TTS) can be swapped, tested, and monitored independently — you can upgrade just the ASR model without touching the rest.
Text is a natural place to insert business logic and guardrails — content filtering, tool-calling, compliance checks — between 'hearing' and 'speaking'.
The tradeoff is latency: three hops instead of one adds up, even if each hop is individually fast.

lessons.title: Speech-to-speech (STS) architecture, in depth
lessons.why: The newer, faster-moving side of the fork — likely to come up if an interviewer wants to test how current your knowledge is.
facts: A single model processes audio in and audio out directly, skipping the text intermediate entirely.
This removes the latency of three separate hops and can produce more natural turn-taking and prosody.
The real cost is inspectability: with no text step, it's much harder to insert guardrails, business logic, or debug exactly why the model said what it said.

lessons.title: Why latency is the whole game
lessons.why: In voice, latency isn't a performance metric — it's the product. A 1.5-second pause reads as broken, not thoughtful.
facts: Human conversation has a natural turn-taking gap of roughly 200ms — anything much longer starts to feel unnatural.
Time-to-first-byte (TTFB) on TTS and streaming (rather than batch) ASR are the two biggest levers for shaving latency.
Deepgram markets sub-300ms STT and sub-200ms TTS as headline numbers — in interviews, expect latency to come up as the primary technical differentiator, not accuracy.
lessons.mustRemember: If asked to compare voice AI vendors, latency budget (not just word error rate) is usually the sharper technical question to ask.

lessons.title: Streaming vs. batch ASR
lessons.why: Confusing these in an interview is an easy tell that you haven't built with the tech.
facts: Streaming ASR transcribes audio continuously as it arrives, word by word — required for any live conversational agent.
Batch ASR processes a complete audio file after the fact — used for things like call transcription, captioning, or analytics, not live dialogue.
Streaming is technically harder: the model must commit to partial transcripts before the speaker has finished, then revise them ('re-scoring') as more audio arrives.

lessons.title: Endpointing
lessons.why: The unglamorous problem that makes or breaks how natural a voice agent feels.
facts: Endpointing is the system deciding "the user has finished speaking."
Too aggressive and it cuts people off mid-sentence; too slow and every exchange feels laggy.
Getting this right is one of the hardest tuning problems in a voice pipeline, precisely because the right answer changes by speaker and context.

lessons.title: Voice activity detection (VAD)
lessons.why: The signal that feeds the endpointing decision — worth knowing as its own named concept.
facts: VAD distinguishes speech from silence or background noise in the audio stream.
It runs continuously and feeds its output into the endpointing decision.
Poor VAD in a noisy environment (a call center floor, a car) is a common real-world failure mode worth naming if asked about edge cases.

lessons.title: Barge-in handling
lessons.why: One of the clearest UX differentiators between a good and a mediocre voice agent.
facts: Barge-in is when a caller interrupts the agent mid-response.
Handling it gracefully means stopping TTS output instantly and re-listening, not finishing the sentence first.
Getting this wrong is one of the fastest ways a voice agent feels robotic rather than conversational.

modules.takeaway: If you remember nothing else: latency budget and the cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech fork are the two things that come up in almost every real conversation about this space.

modules.label: Architecture & Ops
modules.summary: The operational and infra-level decisions that separate "it demos well" from "it's ready for an enterprise deployment."

lessons.title: Where the LLM fits in a voice stack
lessons.why: This connects your existing RAG/agentic-architecture knowledge directly to the voice-specific layer.
facts: The LLM in a voice agent still does the same job as in a chat agent — reasoning, tool-calling, retrieval — but on a much tighter latency budget.
Voice agents often use smaller or distilled models for the first response token, then a larger model for anything that can happen 'in the background' (e.g. logging, summarization).
Function/tool-calling still applies identically — a voice agent booking an appointment is calling the same kind of API a chat agent would.

lessons.title: Diarization and multi-speaker handling
lessons.why: Comes up constantly in enterprise call-center use cases — worth knowing the term cold.
facts: Diarization is labeling 'who said what' in a multi-speaker audio stream (e.g. agent vs. customer, or multiple people on a call).
Critical for call-center analytics, QA, and compliance — not usually needed for a simple 1:1 voice agent.
Accuracy degrades with crosstalk, overlapping speech, and similar-sounding voices — a known limitation worth naming if asked about edge cases.

lessons.title: Deployment models: cloud API vs. on-prem/VPC
lessons.why: Enterprise buyers (Sierra and Deepgram's actual customers) care about this more than raw model quality.
facts: Cloud API: fastest to integrate, usage-based pricing, data leaves the customer's environment.
VPC / self-hosted / on-prem: required for regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) where data residency and compliance are non-negotiable.
Deepgram explicitly sells both — cloud APIs and self-hosted deployments — which is a meaningful differentiator versus API-only competitors.

lessons.title: Accuracy metrics
lessons.why: The first thing most people think to measure — and the one you should lead with least in a business conversation.
facts: Word error rate (WER) for ASR — the percentage of words transcribed wrong.
Task success rate for the agent overall — did it actually accomplish what the caller wanted?
Containment rate — the percentage of calls resolved without human handoff.

lessons.title: Latency metrics
lessons.why: The metric that most directly tracks how the agent *feels* to talk to, not just whether it's technically correct.
facts: Time-to-first-byte (TTFB) on the response — how long before the caller hears anything back.
End-to-end response time — the full round trip from the caller finishing speaking to the agent's audio starting.
Tracked at p50/p90/p99, not just average — a good average with a bad p99 still means real callers hit noticeably laggy moments.

lessons.title: Experience metrics
lessons.why: The hardest to quantify, and often the most predictive of whether users actually trust the agent.
facts: Interruption/barge-in handling rate — how often the agent handles being cut off gracefully versus talking over the caller.
Sentiment trend across the call — whether the caller's tone gets better or worse as the conversation goes on.
Escalation rate to a human agent — related to containment rate, but tracked as its own signal of where the agent's limits are.

modules.takeaway: Containment rate (% of calls resolved without human handoff) is usually the metric enterprise buyers actually care about — lead with it over raw accuracy in a business conversation.

modules.label: Company Positioning
modules.summary: Same underlying knowledge, aimed differently depending on whether you're talking to an infra buyer or a CX buyer.

lessons.title: Deepgram's position in the stack
lessons.why: Understanding exactly what layer a company sells at is the fastest way to sound credible in an interview.
facts: Deepgram is voice AI infrastructure: an API/platform company selling STT, TTS, and a bundled Voice Agent API to developers building on top.
Its customers are typically ISVs and enterprises building their own voice products, not end consumers — it's a picks-and-shovels business.
It differentiates on latency, accuracy in noisy/accented audio, and deployment flexibility (cloud, VPC, on-prem) rather than on having its own branded end-user agent.

lessons.title: Sierra's position in the stack
lessons.why: The contrast with Deepgram is the sharpest way to show you understand the competitive landscape, not just the tech.
facts: Sierra builds branded, vertical conversational agents for enterprises — the finished customer-facing product, not raw infrastructure.
It sells to business/CX leaders (a platform decision), not primarily to developers integrating an API — a different buyer and sales motion than Deepgram.
Sierra's agents span both chat and voice, so infrastructure providers like Deepgram are potential vendors underneath a Sierra-style platform, not direct competitors to it.

lessons.title: Framing your pitch for each interview
lessons.why: The same knowledge base, aimed differently, depending on who's across the table.
facts: For Deepgram (infra company): emphasize your grasp of the technical stack — latency budgets, deployment models, evaluation metrics — since you'd be talking to developers and technical buyers.
For Sierra (applied agent platform): emphasize outcomes and stakeholder management — containment rate, CX impact, rollout strategy — since you'd be talking to business buyers.
In both cases, naming the cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech tradeoff unprompted signals real fluency rather than surface-level familiarity.

modules.takeaway: Naming the cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech tradeoff unprompted, in either interview, signals real fluency rather than surface-level familiarity.

modules.label: Company Specifics
modules.summary: Knowing your interviewer's company's current numbers and trajectory is an easy, high-leverage way to stand out.

lessons.title: Sierra: founding and business
lessons.why: The founding story and customer base tell you exactly what kind of company you're interviewing with.
facts: Founded in early 2024 by Bret Taylor (OpenAI chairman, former Salesforce co-CEO, former Google exec) and Clay Bavor (longtime Google executive) — the two met working together at Google.
Builds branded, vertical conversational agents for enterprises — the finished customer-facing product, not raw infrastructure (see Sierra's position in the stack).
Notable customers include ADT, Sonos, WeightWatchers, and Casper.

lessons.title: Sierra: funding trajectory
lessons.why: The growth curve itself is part of the story — worth knowing the path, not just the current number.
facts: Valued at $1B in January 2024, then $4.5B by October 2024 after raising $175M.
Reached a $10B valuation in September 2025 on a $350M raise.
Raised $950M in May 2026 at a $15.8B valuation, led by Tiger Global and Google's GV — one of the largest AI funding rounds of the year.
lessons.mustRemember: Sierra's valuation roughly tripled from late 2024 to mid-2026 — cite the trajectory, not just the current number, since interviewers reference the growth story.

lessons.title: Deepgram: founding and business
lessons.why: A very different shape of company from Sierra — worth being able to state plainly.
facts: Founded by Scott Stephenson, who remains CEO.
Voice AI infrastructure: sells STT, TTS, and a bundled Voice Agent API to developers (see Deepgram's position in the stack).
Reached roughly $100M ARR in 2026, growing from about 164 employees in 2024 to roughly 310.

lessons.title: Deepgram: funding trajectory
lessons.why: Smaller scale than Sierra, but the investor list itself is worth knowing.
facts: Raised a $130M Series C in January 2026 at a $1.3B valuation, led by AVP.
Existing investors including Alkeon, Madrona, Tiger Global, Y Combinator, and BlackRock-managed funds all joined the round.

New strategic investors in the round included Twilio, ServiceNow Ventures, SAP, and Citi Ventures — worth noting since those are potential integration/distribution partners, not just financial backers.

modules.takeaway: Sierra ($15.8B, May 2026) and Deepgram ($1.3B, Jan 2026) sit at very different scales and buyer types — cite the specific numbers, not just "they're both well-funded," to sound current rather than generic.

modules.label: Interview Practice
modules.summary: The fastest way to fail one of these interviews isn't lacking knowledge — it's failing to translate it into a direct, confident answer under a real question.

lessons.title: Q: Walk me through the components of a voice AI pipeline
lessons.why: A default opening technical question — your chance to immediately signal fluency.
facts: Name the three blocks (ASR, reasoning layer, TTS) and that the dominant production pattern is cascaded, not speech-to-speech.
Volunteer *why* cascaded still dominates — each stage is independently swappable, testable, and monitorable — before being asked.
If time allows, name the speech-to-speech alternative and its tradeoff (lower latency, harder to debug/constrain) to show you know the fork exists.

lessons.title: Q: How would you explain latency's importance to a non-technical stakeholder?
lessons.why: Tests whether you can translate a technical constraint into a business one — a common pivot in these interviews.
facts: Anchor on the ~200ms natural human turn-taking gap — anything much slower reads as "broken," not "thoughtful."
Reframe latency as a product/trust metric, not a performance number — a laggy agent erodes confidence fast, regardless of accuracy.
If pushed for numbers, cite the industry-marketed sub-300ms STT / sub-200ms TTS range as the target, while noting real-world latency also depends on the LLM hop in between.

lessons.title: Q: How would you measure whether a voice agent is actually working?
lessons.why: This is asking you to reproduce the evaluation framework live, not just recite it.
facts: Lead with containment rate (% of calls resolved without human handoff) — the metric enterprise buyers actually care about.
Back it up with accuracy (WER, task success) and latency (p50/p90/p99, not just average) as supporting metrics.
Mention experience-level signals too — barge-in handling, sentiment trend, escalation rate — to show you're not only thinking in raw numbers.

lessons.title: Q: What's the difference in how you'd pitch Sierra vs. Deepgram?
lessons.why: Tests whether you actually understand each company's position, not just its name.
facts: For Deepgram: talk technical stack — latency budgets, deployment flexibility (cloud vs. VPC), evaluation metrics — since you're likely speaking with developers/technical buyers.
For Sierra: talk outcomes — containment rate, CX impact, rollout strategy — since you're likely speaking with business/CX buyers.
In either case, naming the cascaded-vs-speech-to-speech tradeoff unprompted signals fluency rather than surface-level familiarity.

modules.takeaway: Every one of these questions is really testing the same thing: can you connect a technical fact to why it matters to the person asking?
